name: Vitamin A
summary: Vitamin A is needed for seeing in dim light, healthy skin and linings, the immune system and a baby's development. It comes in two kinds: preformed vitamin A (retinol) from animal foods and supplements, and beta-carotene and similar pigments from plants, which the body turns into vitamin A as it needs. Too much preformed vitamin A is harmful, especially in pregnancy.
roles: Vision in dim light (part of the light-sensing pigment in the eye)
Growth and renewal of skin and of the linings of the eyes, gut and airways
Development of the embryo and growth in children

status.note: The usual test is blood (serum) retinol, but the liver keeps it steady over a wide range of stores. It only falls when liver stores are nearly empty, so a normal result doesn't show whether stores are low-ish or high. Infection and inflammation lower it for a while (its carrier, retinol-binding protein, drops), which can look like deficiency. Liver stores are the best measure but are only estimated in research, with isotope tests. Doctors also look at signs such as night blindness. It isn't usually tested without a reason, and this app has no vitamin A marker yet.

signs: Poor vision in dim light (night blindness)
Dry eyes, and in severe cases damage to the front of the eye (xerophthalmia), including foamy spots on the white of the eye (Bitot's spots)
More frequent or more severe infections, especially diarrhoea and measles in children
atRisk: Young children and pregnant women in low- and middle-income countries where diets are poor in vitamin A
People who absorb fat poorly (cystic fibrosis, coeliac disease, pancreas problems, chronic liver disease, after some weight-loss operations)
People eating very restricted diets with few animal foods and few orange or dark green vegetables

signs: After a very large amount at once: headache, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, blurred vision
With high intakes over months: liver damage
With high intakes over years: possible bone weakening and more fractures (the evidence is mixed)
Dry, peeling skin, hair loss, bone and joint pain
Birth defects when intake of preformed vitamin A is high early in pregnancy
Large amounts of beta-carotene can turn the skin yellow-orange; this is harmless and fades
high.note: The harm comes from preformed vitamin A (retinol and retinyl esters) from liver, fish liver oils, fortified foods and supplements, which builds up in the liver. EFSA (the European Food Safety Authority) chose birth defects as the key risk when it set its upper limit, and also reviewed liver damage and bone health. Beta-carotene from plants doesn't cause vitamin A poisoning, because the body converts only what it needs, but beta-carotene supplements carry their own risk: more lung cancer in smokers (see the findings).

examples: Liver and liver products such as pâté and liver sausage (very high in preformed vitamin A)
Cod liver oil and other fish liver oils
Eggs, butter, cheese and whole milk
Fortified spreads and some fortified foods
Beta-carotene: carrots, sweet potato, pumpkin and butternut squash
Beta-carotene: spinach, kale and other dark green leafy vegetables
Beta-carotene: red peppers, mango, apricots and cantaloupe melon
foodSources.note: The measured amounts in this app (CoFID 'retinol') count preformed vitamin A from animal foods only. Beta-carotene and other carotenoids from plants aren't counted there, even though the body turns some of them into vitamin A. EFSA expresses vitamin A as retinol equivalents (RE): 1 µg RE is 1 µg of retinol or 6 µg of beta-carotene.

forms.name: Retinyl palmitate or retinyl acetate (preformed vitamin A)
forms.note: The usual form in supplements and fortified foods. The body uses it directly and stores the excess in the liver, which is why high amounts can build up and cause harm. Labels may give amounts in IU (international units): 1 IU of retinol is 0.3 µg.

forms.name: Beta-carotene (provitamin A)
forms.note: A plant pigment the body converts to vitamin A when it needs it, so it doesn't cause vitamin A poisoning. As a supplement it raised lung cancer in smokers and asbestos workers in large trials; EFSA advises smokers to avoid beta-carotene supplements.

forms.name: Fish liver oils (such as cod liver oil)
forms.note: Contain preformed vitamin A together with vitamin D. The amount varies by product; it adds to vitamin A from other sources.

forms.name: Multivitamins
forms.note: Often contain vitamin A as retinyl esters, beta-carotene or both. The label should say how much of each.

upperLimit.note: Tolerable upper intake level (UL) for preformed vitamin A only (retinol and retinyl esters), in µg retinol equivalents a day from food and supplements together. EFSA re-assessed it in 2024 and kept 3000 µg, with birth defects as the key risk. It applies to men and women, including women who could become pregnant, are pregnant or breastfeeding, and women after menopause. It doesn't cover beta-carotene: EFSA couldn't set a limit for beta-carotene supplements because of the lung cancer risk, saw no sign of harm from beta-carotene in ordinary food, advises smokers to avoid beta-carotene supplements, and says the general population should use them only to meet vitamin A needs. EFSA adds that Europeans are unlikely to go over the limit if they eat liver and liver products once a month or less, and advises women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy not to eat liver products. Intake values (PRI, population reference intake) are in µg retinol equivalents a day; they are guides for groups, not personal targets.

findings.population: Smokers, former smokers and asbestos workers: Finnish male smokers aged 50–69 (ATBC) and US smokers, former smokers and asbestos-exposed workers (CARET)
whyThisGrade: Two large, long, placebo-controlled trials found harm in the same direction
A meta-analysis of trials confirmed more lung cancer at 20–30 mg of beta-carotene a day in smokers and asbestos workers
Applies to beta-carotene supplements, not to carotenoids eaten in food
findings.summary: In the ATBC trial (29,133 male smokers, 5–8 years), men given 20 mg of beta-carotene a day got lung cancer 18% more often than men who weren't, and 8% more died. CARET (18,314 people) gave 30 mg of beta-carotene with retinyl palmitate and was stopped early: 28% more lung cancer and 17% more deaths from any cause. In the AREDS2 eye trial, more lung cancers occurred in people given beta-carotene, mostly former smokers, so it was replaced in the eye formula. Studies of diets rich in carotenoid foods pointed the other way (see the food findings): the classic case of why a food result can't be carried over to a pill.
findings.bottomLine: Two large trials in smokers, former smokers and asbestos workers found more lung cancer with beta-carotene pills: 18% more in one and 28% more in the other, which was stopped early. This applies to the pills; diets rich in carotenoid foods pointed the other way.
findings.label: Beta-carotene: lung cancer
findings.line: 18% and 28% more lung cancer in two trials of smokers and asbestos workers

findings.outcome: Cancer overall and other cancer types (beta-carotene supplements)
findings.population: Adults in nine randomised trials of beta-carotene supplements, healthy or at high risk
whyThisGrade: Nine randomised trials, several large and long
The overall estimate is precise and close to no effect
An independent review for the US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) reached the same conclusion
findings.summary: Beta-carotene supplements didn't lower cancer overall or cancers of the pancreas, bowel, prostate, breast or skin. Stomach cancer, like lung cancer, was more common in smokers and asbestos workers who took them. The USPSTF advises against beta-carotene supplements for preventing heart disease or cancer, judging with moderate certainty that the harms outweigh the benefits.
findings.bottomLine: Across nine trials, beta-carotene pills didn't lower cancer overall or cancers of the pancreas, bowel, prostate, breast or skin. Stomach cancer was more common in smokers and asbestos workers who took them, and a US expert panel judged that the harms outweigh the benefits.
findings.label: Beta-carotene: other cancers
findings.line: No fewer cancers overall; more stomach cancer in smokers and asbestos workers

findings.population: Adults, healthy or with various diseases, in 78 randomised trials of antioxidant supplements
whyThisGrade: Many randomised trials, most at low risk of bias
Doses, combinations and populations differ a lot between trials
The effects are small and depend on which trials are included
findings.summary: In a Cochrane review, trials at low risk of bias showed about 5% more deaths in people given beta-carotene. Preformed vitamin A showed no clear effect overall, but higher doses were linked with more deaths. The review for the USPSTF found beta-carotene linked with about 10% more deaths from heart and blood vessel disease. None of these trials found that the supplements helped people live longer.
findings.bottomLine: A Cochrane review of 78 trials found about 5% more deaths in people given beta-carotene in the most reliable trials. Preformed vitamin A showed no clear effect overall, though higher doses were linked with more deaths. None of the trials found these pills helped people live longer.
findings.label: Death from any cause
findings.line: About 5% more deaths with beta-carotene in the most reliable trials

findings.outcome: Death and illness in young children
findings.population: Children aged 6 months to 5 years, mostly in low- and middle-income countries where vitamin A deficiency is common
whyThisGrade: Cochrane review: 19 trials with over 1.2 million children for deaths, rated high certainty by the reviewers
Only applies where deficiency is common; it says nothing about adults with ordinary European diets
findings.summary: Vitamin A supplements given to young children in community programmes lowered deaths from any cause by about 12% and deaths from diarrhoea by about 12%. They also reduced night blindness, Bitot's spots and vitamin A deficiency. Vomiting in the first two days was more common. This is a public health programme for places where deficiency is widespread, not evidence for well-nourished adults.
findings.bottomLine: In low- and middle-income countries where deficiency is common, vitamin A given to children aged 6 months to 5 years lowered deaths from any cause by about 12%. This is a public health programme for those places, not evidence for well-nourished adults.
findings.label: Child deaths in poorer countries
findings.line: About 12% fewer deaths in children 6 months to 5 years where deficiency is common

studies.title: Vitamin A supplementation for preventing morbidity and mortality in children from six months to five years of age

findings.outcome: Birth defects (preformed vitamin A in early pregnancy)
findings.population: 22,748 pregnant women in the US (a cohort study, not a trial)
whyThisGrade: Observational, so it shows an association; a trial would be unethical
Fits animal studies and the known birth defects caused by vitamin A-like medicines (retinoids)
EFSA chose birth defects as the key risk for its upper limit
findings.summary: Babies of women who took more than 10,000 IU (3,000 µg) of preformed vitamin A a day from supplements had birth defects in tissues that grow from the cranial neural crest (parts of the head, face and heart) about 4.8 times as often as babies of women who took 5,000 IU or less. The extra risk was concentrated in women with high intakes before the seventh week of pregnancy, often before they know they are pregnant. Beta-carotene wasn't part of this finding.
findings.bottomLine: In a study of 22,748 pregnant women in the US, babies of women whose supplements gave more than 10,000 IU (3,000 µg) of preformed vitamin A a day had certain head, face and heart defects about 4.8 times as often. It was a cohort study, not a trial, and beta-carotene wasn't part of it.
findings.label: Birth defects (early pregnancy)
findings.line: Certain birth defects about 4.8 times as often with high preformed vitamin A; one cohort study

foodFindings.population: Adults in 25 prospective cohort studies (observational, not trials)
whyThisGrade: Observational: shows an association, not cause and effect
Eating many carotenoids also marks eating more fruit and vegetables and smoking less, which is hard to adjust away
The trials that tested beta-carotene pills found no benefit, and harm in smokers
foodFindings.summary: People who ate the most carotenoids, or had the highest blood levels, tended to get somewhat less lung cancer, even after allowing for smoking. The differences were generally small and many weren't statistically clear. The same review found that beta-carotene supplements didn't lower lung cancer. A carotenoid-rich diet and a beta-carotene pill are different things, and the pill result is the one tested in trials.
foodFindings.bottomLine: In 25 observational studies, people who ate the most carotenoids tended to get somewhat less lung cancer, even allowing for smoking. The differences were small and often not statistically clear, and the same review found that beta-carotene pills didn't lower lung cancer.
foodFindings.label: Eating carotenoids: lung cancer
foodFindings.line: Somewhat less lung cancer in observational studies; differences small and uncertain

interactions.note: High intakes of preformed vitamin A early in pregnancy are linked with birth defects. EFSA advises women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy not to eat liver or liver products, and this app hides foods with 300 µg of retinol or more per portion in pregnancy. Beta-carotene from vegetables isn't counted in the limit. Talk to a doctor or midwife about any supplement in pregnancy.

These medicines are related to vitamin A, so vitamin A supplements add to their side effects. They also cause birth defects. Ask the prescriber or a pharmacist before using any vitamin A supplement with them.

interactions.with: Smoking now or in the past, and asbestos exposure
interactions.note: Beta-carotene supplements raised lung cancer in smokers and asbestos workers, and in former smokers in one eye trial. EFSA advises smokers to avoid beta-carotene supplements. Carotenoids from food weren't linked with this.

interactions.with: Liver disease or heavy alcohol use
interactions.note: The liver stores vitamin A, and a damaged liver is more easily harmed by high amounts. Discuss any vitamin A supplement with your doctor.

interactions.with: Orlistat and conditions with poor fat absorption
interactions.note: Vitamin A is fat-soluble. Orlistat (a weight-loss medicine) and conditions that reduce fat absorption lower how much is absorbed. A doctor can check whether this matters.

cautions: Preformed vitamin A adds up across supplements, fish liver oils, fortified foods and liver.
Vitamin A and beta-carotene are different: a 'plant form' supplement isn't automatically safe for smokers.
Labels may use IU (international units); 1 IU of retinol is 0.3 µg.
Sudden headache, blurred vision or vomiting after high-dose vitamin A, or yellowing of the eyes, needs a doctor.
Before using a supplement in pregnancy, or with a liver condition, discuss it with your doctor.
